First, as the authors note, PIF4 can heterodimerize/oligomerize with other bHLH proteins. In vivo, PIF4 mutant alleles (mTAD, mB, RRQQ) could dimerize/oligomerize with other PIFs (PIF1/3/4/5/7), thereby binding DNA and activating gene expression. Indeed, the authors showed that mTAD is functional in the pif4 mutant background (Fig. 3) but not in the pif1/3/4/5 background (Fig. 8). A simple explanation is that transactivation activity is supplied by heterodimerized/oligomerized PIFs, which suggests that transactivation activity is in fact necessary. The same reasoning applies to DNA-binding activity. To test this, please also include PIF7, which is known to play an important role in thermomorphogenesis.
Response: Thank you for the thoughtful critique. We believe there is a misunderstanding of our conclusion. We did not claim that transactivation or DNA binding are unnecessary for thermomorphogenesis; rather, we concluded that PIF4’s own TAD- and DBD-mediated contributions are minor/dispensable in vivo under our conditions when oligomerization partners are present.
Our data explicitly support this partner-dependent model: the mTAD allele retains function in the pif4 background (Fig. 3) but fails in the pifq (pif1345) background (Fig. 8). As the reviewer mentioned, these outcomes are most parsimoniously explained by functional compensation via HLH-mediated hetero-oligomerization, whereby partner PIFs (and potentially other activators) supply sufficient transactivation and DNA-binding capacity. In other words, transactivation and DNA binding remain necessary at the network level, but PIF4’s intrinsic TAD/DBD are not strictly required so long as partner factors are available. Conversely, when key partners are removed (as in the pifq background), compensation is lost and the requirement for PIF4’s TAD becomes evident—fully consistent with our interpretation. We realized that our original submission showed only how PIF4 variants affected its homo-oligomerization. To strengthen our argument that PIF4 HLH also mediates its hetero-oligomerization with other PIFs, we performed GST pulldown assays and demonstrated that the mBH variant also dramatically reduced the interaction between PIF4 and some other PIFs (e.g., PIF3 and PIF5), whereas the mB and mTAD versions failed to (Supplementary Fig. 7). We also modified the Results section to emphasize these new data (lines 429-440).
When many readers hear “functional redundancy,” they think of classic gene-level redundancy—loss of one gene is compensated for by other related (most likely homologous) genes. Our case is different. PIF4 itself is essential for thermomorphogenesis (the pif4 null shows a strong defect), but when PIF4 is present, HLH-mediated oligomerization allows it to recruit partner factors (e.g., other PIFs). Those partners’ TADs and DBDs can supply transactivation and DNA binding, making PIF4’s own TAD/DBD dispensable under those conditions, while oligomerization remains critical. In the pifq background, where key partners are absent, this compensation is lost, and PIF4’s TAD becomes required for target gene expression at warm temperatures (Fig. 8). We discuss these distinctions in detail in the original manuscript’s Discussion sections: “Contribution of the TAD to PIF4-dependent gene expression at warm temperatures” (lines 471-519), “Contribution of PIF4’s DBD to its role in thermosensory gene expression” (lines 521-553), and “Contribution of oligomerization to PIF4’s role in thermomorphogenesis” (lines 555-582).
We totally agree that PIF7 is important for thermomorphogenesis. Unfortunately, we didn’t have the pif13457 quintuple mutant at hand when generating the transgenic lines. Besides, when we tested whether PIF4 variants would affect its hetero-oligomerization with other PIFs, we could easily detect PIF4’s interaction with PIF3 and PIF5 (Supplementary Fig. 7) but failed to see PIF4-PIF7 interaction using the GST pulldown assay. These results really puzzled us as PIF4 was reported to interact with PIF7 in yeast two-hybrid assays2. However, given that the mTAD variant of PIF4 failed to promote thermosensory hypocotyl growth in pifq (Fig. 8), our argument that PIF4’s TAD function is dispensable while other PIFs are present but is required when its partners are absent is well supported. Therefore, we think the pifq data is sufficient, and it’s not necessary to include PIF7 to strengthen our conclusion.
10. The authors suggest that PIF4’s HLH domain might possess unique properties that support heterotypic oligomerization with non-PIF cofactors during thermomorphogenesis. However, as I remember, a previously report (Kim et al(?) (2024) Plant Cell) demonstrated that the C-terminal domains of PIF1 and PIF4 are interchangeable, indicating that unique HLH characteristics are unlikely.
Response: Thank you for raising this. We agree with the reviewer’s interpretation and have already discussed it in the original manuscript’s Discussion section, “Condensate-independent roles of the PIF4 N-terminal IDR in thermomorphogenesis” (lines 624-635). There, we cite the 2024 Plant Cell paper from Giltsu Choi’s group, which shows that the C-terminal regions of PIF1 and PIF4 are interchangeable14. Consistent with that work, our view is that the HLH module is necessary for dimerization/oligomerization but does not confer unique heterotypic specificity; instead, recruitment of non-PIF cofactors during thermomorphogenesis is more plausibly mediated by features within the PIF4 N-terminal IDR.
We think the confusion comes from the last paragraph in one of the Discussion sections, titled “Contribution of oligomerization to PIF4’s role in thermomorphogenesis,” where we listed three potential PIF4-specific features that might determine its central role in thermomorphogenesis. The statement that “PIF4’s HLH might possess unique characteristics that support heterotypic oligomerization with non-PIF cofactors” was the 2nd feature described there. Even though we added a sentence, saying “we will discuss this further in the last section,” we now realize that it created confusion. As mentioned above, our discussion on Choi’s data in a later section basically rejects this possibility. Therefore, we modified these sentences by saying “PIF4 might possess unique structural characteristics that broaden its multivalent interaction capacity with non-PIF cofactors” (lines 578-579).

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1: The authors have addressed all my concerns.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
Many of my previous concerns have been addressed properly. However, I think some parts of the manuscript remain misleading and require further clarification. My comments are as follows:
FRAP assay: In my previous review, I was referring to the nucleoplasmic GFP signal not cytosolic signal. The figures show that both the condensate and the surrounding nucleoplasmic signals recover only marginally. This raises concerns about the authors’ conclusion that PIF4 forms gel-like condensates. The authors should either provide additional data supporting this conclusion or revise it accordingly.
Figure 3 title and lines 247/248: The current title, “PIF4 TAD is largely dispensable…”, is misleading. Since the authors clarified that this is not their intended meaning—that the TAD is still necessary but may be supplied by other oligomerized PIFs in planta—I recommend revising the description. Alternatively, the authors could insert a phrase directing readers to relevant sections of the manuscript, such as lines 432–435 or the discussion (lines 555–582). Similarly, the authors should review other instances in the main text and supplemental materials where “dispensable” or “not necessary” is used.
Title in line 381 and subsequent descriptions: Similar concerns apply here. The current phrasing is highly misleading. As with the TAD, the authors should clarify that DNA-binding activity may be contributed by other PIFs.
Lines 450–454: This section is also highly misleading, or possibly incorrect. As shown in Figure 8e, PIF4 is fully functional in the absence of at least four other PIFs, indicating that hetero-oligomerization is not required for its function. Moreover, mBH lacks both oligomerization and DNA-binding activity, and the function of RRQQ has not been tested in pifQ or pifP. Therefore, the authors cannot claim that the PIF4 dimer is non-functional. Ideally, the authors should test whether PIF4 variants that retain all activities except (hetero-)oligomerization remain functional or not in pifQ or pifP mutants before concluding that a PIF4 (hetero-)oligomer, but not a dimer, is functional. Without such data, the model in Figure 8f should be revised, and all related misleading descriptions in the text should be carefully reworded.
Figure S7: For “PIF4mB” and “PIF4mBH,” should mB and mBH be formatted as superscripts?

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
The authors have addressed all my concerns.
Response: Thank you for your comment.
Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
Many of my previous concerns have been addressed properly. However, I think some parts of the manuscript remain misleading and require further clarification. My comments are as follows:
Response: Thank you for pointing out these issues. Please see our responses below.
1. FRAP assay: In my previous review, I was referring to the nucleoplasmic GFP signal not cytosolic signal. The figures show that both the condensate and the surrounding nucleoplasmic signals recover only marginally. This raises concerns about the authors’ conclusion that PIF4 forms gel-like condensates. The authors should either provide additional data supporting this conclusion or revise it accordingly.
Response: Thank you for the clarification. We agree with the reviewer. The observation that both the condensates and the surrounding nucleoplasm recover only marginally suggests that nuclear mobility of PIF4 is globally low under our assay conditions. Such FRAP profiles are not, by themselves, diagnostic of a gel-like material state and are equally consistent with binding-dominated or supply-limited regimes (e.g., a small mobile fraction caused by strong chromatin tethering and/or slow nuclear import). Accordingly, we have revised the manuscript to replace “gel-like” with “low-mobility” condensates throughout, and we have added a few sentences to the Discussion section (lines 594–599) to explain this limitation of FRAP and clarify our interpretation.
2. Figure 3 title and lines 247/248: The current title, “PIF4 TAD is largely dispensable…”, is misleading. Since the authors clarified that this is not their intended meaning—that the TAD is still necessary but may be supplied by other oligomerized PIFs in planta—I recommend revising the description. Alternatively, the authors could insert a phrase directing readers to relevant sections of the manuscript, such as lines 432–435 or the discussion (lines 555–582). Similarly, the authors should review other instances in the main text and supplemental materials where “dispensable” or “not necessary” is used.
Response: Thank you for the suggestion; we appreciate the opportunity to clarify our intent. Our use of “dispensable” referred specifically to PIF4’s own TAD in a wild-type background, where partners (e.g., other PIFs) are present and can compensate via high-order oligomerization. In that context, TAD mutations (mTAD, mWFYL) produce only minor effects on thermoresponsive hypocotyl elongation (Fig. 3j–n; Fig. 5g–k). Importantly, we are not suggesting that transactivation is unnecessary for thermomorphogenesis; rather, we conclude that PIF4’s intrinsic TAD can be omitted because transactivation is supplied by oligomerized partners when the network is intact. We summarized the wild-type and TAD mutant PIF4 models in Fig. R1a and R1b, respectively.
An analogy may help. Consider a structure supported by multiple pillars: each pillar contributes to stability, but the building remains standing if any single pillar is removed. Under those conditions, one could say an individual pillar is “dispensable” because the design includes redundancy. However, if several pillars are removed and the structure is near failure, removing one more pillar will cause collapse. This mirrors our genetic tests: in pifq, where four key partners are absent, redundancy is largely eliminated, and PIF4’s TAD becomes required for target gene expression at warm temperatures (Fig. 8b–e). By contrast, the wild-type background reflects the natural, redundant network in which the TAD’s contribution can be supplied by partners.
That said, we recognize that the word “dispensable” can be misread when stripped of its context (e.g., in a figure title). To avoid ambiguity, we have revised the language to describe the observed effects without the deductive label and to point readers to the partner-dependent model. Specifically, the Fig. 3 title is now: “Loss-of-function mutations in the PIF4 TAD modestly affect thermomorphogenesis.” We have also reviewed the text and Supplementary Information to ensure that any remaining uses of “dispensable” and “not necessary” are tightly qualified by the genetic context or replaced with descriptive phrasing.
3. Title in line 381 and subsequent descriptions: Similar concerns apply here. The current phrasing is highly misleading. As with the TAD, the authors should clarify that DNA-binding activity may be contributed by other PIFs.
Response: Thank you again for the suggestion. Similar to our response to the previous comment, the use of “not required” referred only to PIF4’s intrinsic DNA-binding capacity in a wild-type context with partner PIFs present. We do not imply that DNA binding is unnecessary for thermomorphogenesis overall. Rather, our data support a partner-dependent model in which hetero-oligomerized PIFs supply sufficient DNA-binding activity, allowing PIF4 variants with impaired DBD to retain function in the pif4 background (comparing Fig. R1a and Fig. R1c). From this perspective, our interpretation agrees with the reviewer’s.
To improve clarity, we revised the section title and accompanying text. The title now reads “Disrupting PIF4’s DNA-binding ability modestly affects thermomorphogenesis,” a descriptive formulation that reports the result without overinterpretation, allowing readers to assess the implications in context. We also explicitly state that PIF4’s partners, such as other PIFs, may contribute DNA-binding activity (lines 409-411).
4. Lines 450–454: This section is also highly misleading, or possibly incorrect. As shown in Figure 8e, PIF4 is fully functional in the absence of at least four other PIFs, indicating that hetero-oligomerization is not required for its function. Moreover, mBH lacks both oligomerization and DNA-binding activity, and the function of RRQQ has not been tested in pifQ or pifP. Therefore, the authors cannot claim that the PIF4 dimer is non-functional. Ideally, the authors should test whether PIF4 variants that retain all activities except (hetero-)oligomerization remain functional or not in pifQ or pifP mutants before concluding that a PIF4 (hetero-)oligomer, but not a dimer, is functional. Without such data, the model in Figure 8f should be revised, and all related misleading descriptions in the text should be carefully reworded.
Response: Thank you for the comment. Since your points touch several issues, we will address them in turn while keeping our logic explicit.
First, on whether PIF4 is “fully functional” in the absence of four PIFs (PIF1/3/4/5). What counts as “functional” depends on the benchmark. If the term refers to biochemical activity, we agree that PIF4 retains function on its own—in pifq, transgenic PIF4 could still elevate IAA19/IAA29 at 27 °C (original Fig. 8e). That’s also the reason we used the pifq background to test the notion that PIF4’s own TAD would become more important when its partners are absent (please refer to the “pillar” analogy in our response to Comment #2). Please note that PIF4 could still form homo-oligomers in the pifq background, and thus, the gene activation in the pifq background does not necessarily mean that PIF4’s activity is achieved in the form of dimers. On the other hand, if “fully functional” means restoration to wild-type output in Arabidopsis, our data do not support that interpretation. In Fig. 8c, neither PIF4/pifq line (#24 or #4) restores hypocotyl length to Col-0 when transgene expression matches wild type (Fig. 8b). To make this explicit, we repeated the RT-qPCR in Fig. 8e with Col-0 controls. In the revised Fig. 8e, PIF4 could still induce IAA19/IAA29 in the pifq background at 27 °C, but both transcripts remain well below Col-0, consistent with the partial hypocotyl rescue. Thus, PIF4 is active in pifq but not fully functional relative to the wild-type benchmark, indicating that PIF4’s full strength in planta requires partner PIFs.
Second, on whether “the PIF4 dimer is non-functional.” We want to clarify that we did not claim that PIF4 dimers are non-functional in the manuscript. Our point is that PIF4’s thermomorphogenetic output relies on its ability to recruit partners. In the first seven figures and supplementary figures, alleles that disrupt PIF4’s own TAD or DBD—mTAD, mWFYL, mB, RRQQ—still largely or fully complement pif4, implying that partner factors can supply DNA binding and/or transactivation when PIF4’s intrinsic modules are compromised (functional redundancy at the complex level). We considered that two candidate features of PIF4—the HLH oligomerization module and the N-terminal IDR—could potentially mediate protein-protein interactions required for partner recruitment. While we haven’t obtained any data to support IDR’s contribution, our mB and mBH data are informative here to support the involvement of the HLH oligomerization domain (Fig. R1a,c,d). If PIF4 functioned strictly as a self-contained dimer without partners, mB (defective basic region) would be unable to bind DNA—either as an mB–mB homodimer or an mB–“other PIF” heterodimer—because bHLH dimers require two functional basic regions to engage DNA1. Yet mB complements pif4 (Fig. 7e–h), arguing that PIF4, in a dimer format, can recruit partners that contribute the necessary DNA-binding capacity. Building on mB, we then disrupted higher-order oligomerization with mBH (basic + HLH). mBH fails to complement pif4 (Fig. 7a–d), and our GST pulldown assays (Supplementary Fig. 7a) show reduced PIF4–PIF interactions, indicating that loss of oligomerization competence abolishes this partner-enabled compensation. We agree with the reviewer that a PIF4 variant that retains all activities except oligomerization will be useful. However, we are not trying to claim that high-order (hetero-)oligomerization is PIF4’s ONLY path to partner recruitment in this manuscript. Additional regions—such as the N-terminal IDR—may also participate, as reflected in our model in Fig. 8f and discussed in the section “Condensate-independent roles of the PIF4 N-terminal IDR in thermomorphogenesis” (lines 630-651). While we are actively testing the IDR’s contribution to PIF4-mediated thermomorphogenesis, our conclusion at present is narrower: oligomerization ability is crucial for PIF4’s thermomorphogenetic function but might not be the only contributor.
Third, by integrating the full dataset rather than treating each result in isolation, our objective is to define the structural determinants of PIF4’s thermomorphogenetic function. The evidence collectively supports a partner-dependent model in which PIF4 must be present (the pif4 null shows strong defects), but its intrinsic TAD/DBD contributions can be compensated when interaction partners are available. Importantly, these partners are not limited to PIFs; we use the pifq background as a reductionist model to partially remove functional redundancy and show that, in the absence of several key PIFs, PIF4’s own TAD becomes more consequential—when mutated, PIF4 fails to activate thermosensory gene expression. We are not asserting that PIFs are the only partners, nor that the HLH oligomerization module is the sole interface for partner recruitment. It is highly plausible that the N-terminal IDR also mediates compensatory interactions with non-PIF cofactors; indeed, the PIF1–PIF4 domain-swap study from Giltsu Choi’s group suggests a unique role for the PIF4 N-terminus in thermo-induced hypocotyl elongation2. We also mentioned in the Fig. 8f legend that PIF4’s N-terminus is known to interact with multiple cofactors, such as HSFA1d, MED25, HMR, and MRG2. Going forward, we will dissect how PIF4 engages its partners—PIF and non-PIF alike—and test whether specific IDR segments make major contributions to these interactions.
Recognizing that oligomerization may not be the sole determinant of PIF4 function, we softened the Fig. 8 title to: “PIF4 oligomerization ability is crucial for its thermomorphogenetic function.” We also clarified the Fig. 8 legend: the cross indicates conditions in which PIF4-mediated thermosensory hypocotyl growth is not detectably affected when a given function (intrinsic DNA-binding) is disrupted, whereas the check mark indicates impaired growth under the corresponding disruption (oligomerization).
5. Figure S7: For “PIF4mB” and “PIF4mBH,” should mB and mBH be formatted as superscripts?
Response: Thank you for the suggestion. We confirm that mB and mBH are formatted as superscripts in Supplementary Fig. 7 and its legend, consistent with other variants (mTAD, mWFYL, mDE, RRQQ). During this check, we noticed that Fig. 6 used the labels mKRALL, mKRNLS, mKRBH, and mKRB. To standardize nomenclature and avoid confusion, we have renamed these variants to mALL, mNLS, mBH, and mB, respectively (lines 343–353), and we format them as superscripts when appended to PIF4 (e.g., PIF4mALL, PIF4mNLS, PIF4mBH, and PIF4mB). The text, figures, legends, and supplementary materials have been updated accordingly.
References
1. Voronova, A. & Baltimore, D. Mutations that disrupt DNA binding and dimer formation in the E47 helix-loop-helix protein map to distinct domains. Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. U. S. A. 87, 4722–4726 (1990).
2. Kim, H., Lee, N., Kim, Y. & Choi, G. The phytochrome-interacting factor genes PIF1 and PIF4 are functionally diversified due to divergence of promoters and proteins. Plant Cell (2024) doi:10.1093/plcell/koae110.
We thank the reviewer #2 again for allowing us to explain our data further and refine our conclusions. In the revised manuscript, we have made our best effort to improve our statements and have implemented changes in the text, figures, figure legends, and supplementary data.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
I think authors still need to edit a few parts to avoid misleading readers (or to avoid overstatement).
1. Figures 8c–e show that PIF4/pifq is functional, whereas PIF4mTAD/pifq is not. These data clearly indicate that PIF4 can function even in the absence of at least three other PIFs, thus suggesting that PIF4 can work as a homodimer or homooligomer. When functioning as a homodimer/oligomer, PIF4 requires its own transactivation domain (TAD). Similarly, although the authors have not experimentally tested this, it is highly likely that PIF4mB/pifq would also be nonfunctional due to the lack of DNA-binding activity, as homodimeric/homooligomeric PIF4 would require its own DNA-binding domain (DBD).
I believe the authors also agree with this interpretation, based on the overall logic of the manuscript and their response letter. My concern is that several statements in the manuscript give the impression that PIF4 does not require a TAD or DBD and does not function as a dimer. A few examples of misleading parts are:
2. Authors retain the original title: “PIF4-mediated thermomorphogenesis relies on its oligomerization ability, not DNA-binding or transactivation activity.” This title gives the impression that DNA binding and transactivation activities of PIF4 are not necessary.
3. Authors state in the abstract: “By contrast, replacing three conserved basic residues in the first helix of the HLH domain disrupts PIF4 oligomerization and abolishes thermo-induced hypocotyl growth. We conclude that the ability of PIF4 to oligomerize, rather than to bind DNA or recruit the transcriptional machinery, is the primary determinant of its thermomorphogenetic activity.”
Authors did not mutate only three amino acids; rather, they mutated both DNA-binding and helix sequences (mBH). To reach this conclusion, the authors would need to show that a PIF4 variant lacking only oligomerization activity is nonfunctional in the pifq background. In addition, although it was not tested, it is likely that PIF4mB/pifq would also be nonfunctional, just as PIF4mTAD/pifq was nonfunctional. Therefore, the authors cannot conclusively state that “the ability of PIF4 to oligomerize, rather than to bind DNA or recruit the transcriptional machinery, is the primary determinant of its thermomorphogenetic activity.”
Based on the overall logic of the manuscript and the response letter, I think the authors intend to argue that the DBD and TAD are still essential but can be supplied in trans by other PIFs, provided that PIF4 can oligomerize. The same concern applies to several other parts of the manuscript, including the last sentence of the Introduction and the first sentence of the Discussion.
4. A similar issue applies to the necessity of condensate-forming ability, as the authors have not shown that PIF4mWFYL is functional in the pifq background. I will not elaborate on this point, but the authors may wish to be more cautious here as well, because other oligomerized PIFs could provide intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) (PIF4mWFYL expressed in wild-type transgenic Arabidopsis could still form condensates in transgenic Arabidopsis because of other oligomerized PIFs’ IDRs).
5. The model in Fig. 8f depicts a PIF4 dimer bound to target DNA with an “X” mark and PIF4 multimers with a “check” mark. The figure legend states that the “X” mark indicates “is not affected when such a function is disrupted,” whereas the “check” mark indicates “is affected when such a function is disrupted.” Again, this presentation gives the impression that PIF4 does not require its DNA-binding domain and does not function as a dimer.
6. A similar concern applies to the last sentence of the Results: “Collectively, these data support the notion that the central role of PIF4 in thermomorphogenesis hinges on HLH-mediated hetero-oligomerization with partner factors (e.g., other PIFs), whereas its other canonical TF features, including transactivation and DNA-binding activities, contribute only marginally to thermosensory growth.”
The authors cannot conclusively state that thermomorphogenesis “hinges on hetero-oligomerization”, because they did not demonstrate that PIF4 dimers are nonfunctional. Instead, they showed that either PIF4 dimers and/or PIF4 homooligomers are functional in pifq background (Fig. 8e) and PIF4mTAD (presumably PIF4mB) are not functional in pifq background and in that context, canonical features of transcription factor are required.

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
Response: Thank you for emphasizing these issues. Please see our responses below.
1. Figures 8c–e show that PIF4/pifq is functional, whereas PIF4mTAD/pifq is not. These data clearly indicate that PIF4 can function even in the absence of at least three other PIFs, thus suggesting that PIF4 can work as a homodimer or homooligomer. When functioning as a homodimer/oligomer, PIF4 requires its own transactivation domain (TAD). Similarly, although the authors have not experimentally tested this, it is highly likely that PIF4mB/pifq would also be nonfunctional due to the lack of DNA-binding activity, as homodimeric/homooligomeric PIF4 would require its own DNA-binding domain (DBD).
I believe the authors also agree with this interpretation, based on the overall logic of the manuscript and their response letter. My concern is that several statements in the manuscript give the impression that PIF4 does not require a TAD or DBD and does not function as a dimer. A few examples of misleading parts are:
Response: Thank you for the explanation again. We agree with the reviewer’s prediction that PIF4mB would likely be nonfunctional in the pifq background. However, PIF4/pifq versus PIF4mTAD/pifq contrast alone might not imply that PIF4 acts strictly as a homodimer/homooligomer. The pifq background removes PIF1/3/5, but not all potential partners; other PIFs (e.g., PIF7, as the reviewer mentioned in previous revisions) and non-PIF cofactors (e.g., TCP51) could still assemble with PIF4 and contribute TAD/DBD function. Our use of pifq was a reductionist test to show that when partner availability is reduced, PIF4’s own TAD becomes consequential—hence PIF4mTAD is less functional in pifq. On the contrary, in the pif4 single-mutant background, TAD (and probably DBD) mutations do not abrogate PIF4’s function because partner compensation remains available.
We appreciate that these findings may feel counterintuitive, especially given the classic view that transcription factors rely on their own DNA-binding and transactivation modules. Our data led us to a partner-dependent model: in a wild-type context, PIF4 variants with disrupted TAD (e.g., mTAD and mWFYL) or DBD (e.g., mB and RRQQ) still support thermo-induced hypocotyl elongation, consistent with compensation from interacting factors when oligomerization is intact. From the reviewer’s comments in this and previous revisions, we believe the reviewer also agrees with this model.
That being said, we understand the reviewer’s concern that readers may misinterpret our conclusions. Therefore, we have softened our statements or modified the expression following the reviewer’s suggestions. The detailed changes are pasted in our response to each comment below.
As for the oligomerization and dimer function part, we agree with the reviewer that our data has its limitations. We will explain these in detail below, and related changes in the manuscript will be discussed in our response to each comment.
2. Authors retain the original title: “PIF4-mediated thermomorphogenesis relies on its oligomerization ability, not DNA-binding or transactivation activity.” This title gives the impression that DNA binding and transactivation activities of PIF4 are not necessary.
Response: Thank you for pointing this out. We have changed the title to “Oligomerization-competent PIF4 drives thermomorphogenesis through functional redundancy in transactivation and DNA binding.” We believe this title reflects the results more accurately: 1) it emphasizes that the oligomerization function of PIF4 is crucial for thermomorphogenesis without denying the possibility that the dimer form of PIF4 may also contribute, and 2) it implies that PIF4’s partners are contributing to thermo-induced gene expression through their transactivation and DNA-binding activities instead of implying that PIF4’s own transactivation and DNA-binding activities do not play a role in this process.
3. Authors state in the abstract: “By contrast, replacing three conserved basic residues in the first helix of the HLH domain disrupts PIF4 oligomerization and abolishes thermo-induced hypocotyl growth. We conclude that the ability of PIF4 to oligomerize, rather than to bind DNA or recruit the transcriptional machinery, is the primary determinant of its thermomorphogenetic activity.”
Authors did not mutate only three amino acids; rather, they mutated both DNA-binding and helix sequences (mBH). To reach this conclusion, the authors would need to show that a PIF4 variant lacking only oligomerization activity is nonfunctional in the pifq background. In addition, although it was not tested, it is likely that PIF4mB/pifq would also be nonfunctional, just as PIF4mTAD/pifq was nonfunctional. Therefore, the authors cannot conclusively state that “the ability of PIF4 to oligomerize, rather than to bind DNA or recruit the transcriptional machinery, is the primary determinant of its thermomorphogenetic activity.”
Based on the overall logic of the manuscript and the response letter, I think the authors intend to argue that the DBD and TAD are still essential but can be supplied in trans by other PIFs, provided that PIF4 can oligomerize. The same concern applies to several other parts of the manuscript, including the last sentence of the Introduction and the first sentence of the Discussion.
Response: Thank you for the detailed comments. Indeed, these statements in the abstract, introduction, and discussion were not accurate. The reviewer’s interpretation of our central message is sound.
We have changed the statement in the abstract (lines 42–47) to “By contrast, substituting twelve basic residues within the basic motif and first helix of the HLH domain, which disrupts both DNA binding and HLH-mediated oligomerization, abolishes thermo-induced hypocotyl growth. These findings support a model in which PIF4’s oligomerization competence contributes significantly to thermomorphogenesis by enabling partner recruitment, allowing DNA-binding and transactivation functions to be supplied in trans.”
We have changed the last sentence of the Introduction (lines 123–129) to “By contrast, substituting twelve basic residues, nine in the basic motif and three in the first helix of PIF4’s HLH domain, abolishes higher-order oligomerization and extinguishes thermomorphogenetic growth. We therefore propose a partner-dependent model of PIF4-mediated thermomorphogenetic regulation, in which PIF4’s ability to oligomerize—potentially aided by its long N-terminal IDR—enables recruitment of cofactors that can supply DNA-binding and transactivation in trans.”
We have changed the first paragraph of the Discussion (lines 461–476) to “Eukaryotic TFs are traditionally defined by two capacities—sequence-specific DNA recognition and cofactor recruitment, both of which are critical for gene expression modulation. Although PIF4, a canonical bHLH TF, carries the expected machinery for both tasks—an arginine-rich DNA-binding motif and an acidic TAD—our results indicate that in contexts where partner factors are available, PIF4 variants with disrupted DNA-binding or transactivation activity still support thermosensory gene expression and hypocotyl growth, consistent with partner-enabled compensation. Moreover, these two motifs form part of a long N-terminal IDR that promotes PIF4 phase separation in vitro and in planta, but mutations that reduce condensation did not impair PIF4 function under our assay conditions. By contrast, a combined basic-region/first-helix substitution that disrupts both DNA binding and HLH-mediated oligomerization abolishes thermomorphogenetic output, underscoring the importance of oligomerization competence when intrinsic TAD/DBD inputs cannot be supplied by cofactors in trans. We therefore propose that PIF4 drives thermomorphogenesis by assembling multi-protein complexes—likely including PIFs and non-PIF cofactors—such that DNA-binding and transactivation inputs can be provided by partners, while the exact stoichiometry of the active assembly remains to be determined.”
4. A similar issue applies to the necessity of condensate-forming ability, as the authors have not shown that PIF4mWFYL is functional in the pifq background. I will not elaborate on this point, but the authors may wish to be more cautious here as well, because other oligomerized PIFs could provide intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) (PIF4mWFYL expressed in wild-type transgenic Arabidopsis could still form condensates in transgenic Arabidopsis because of other oligomerized PIFs’ IDRs).
Response: Thank you for raising this point. It is well taken and has been partially addressed in our response to reviewer comment #8 in the 1st revision. We understand the concern as follows: in a wild-type, partner-sufficient context, PIF4mWFYL may still participate in condensates because co-oligomerizing partners (such as other PIFs) contribute their own IDRs, thereby enabling co-condensation in trans. Therefore, it’s not surprising that the mWFYL variant could still complement pif4, as it could still phase separate with co-oligomerizing partners aided by their IDRs. We agree that this is plausible, although we were unable to evaluate PIF4mWFYL condensates directly in Arabidopsis due to weak fluorescence in stable lines (explained in our responses in the 1st revision and mentioned in the revised manuscript).
Our phase-separation assays—especially the in vitro experiments with recombinant protein—measure PIF4’s intrinsic propensity to form condensates. Our claim is that this intrinsic condensation capacity is not a limiting factor for PIF4’s thermomorphogenetic function under our conditions. We are not suggesting that PIF4 forms condensates only with itself. As with DNA binding and transactivation, condensation can also be supplied in trans by partner factors—such as other PIFs—within mixed assemblies.
To incorporate the reviewer’s point, we have revised the Discussion section, “Low-mobility PIF4 condensates and their role in thermal responses.” The last sentence (lines 620–623) now reads: “Thus, in wild-type plants, PIF4’s intrinsic phase-separation propensity is not rate-limiting for thermosensory hypocotyl growth, with condensate features potentially supplied in trans by partner IDRs (e.g., other PIFs and TCPs).”
5. The model in Fig. 8f depicts a PIF4 dimer bound to target DNA with an “X” mark and PIF4 multimers with a “check” mark. The figure legend states that the “X” mark indicates “is not affected when such a function is disrupted,” whereas the “check” mark indicates “is affected when such a function is disrupted.” Again, this presentation gives the impression that PIF4 does not require its DNA-binding domain and does not function as a dimer.
Response: Thank you. We decided to remove all the marks beside PIF4’s structural features. Corresponding descriptions in the Figure 8f legends have also been deleted (after line 1261).
6. A similar concern applies to the last sentence of the Results: “Collectively, these data support the notion that the central role of PIF4 in thermomorphogenesis hinges on HLH-mediated hetero-oligomerization with partner factors (e.g., other PIFs), whereas its other canonical TF features, including transactivation and DNA-binding activities, contribute only marginally to thermosensory growth.”
The authors cannot conclusively state that thermomorphogenesis “hinges on hetero-oligomerization”, because they did not demonstrate that PIF4 dimers are nonfunctional. Instead, they showed that either PIF4 dimers and/or PIF4 homooligomers are functional in pifq background (Fig. 8e) and PIF4mTAD (presumably PIF4mB) are not functional in pifq background and in that context, canonical features of transcription factor are required.
Response: Our view is not contradictory to the reviewer’s. As we explained in our response to reviewer comment #4 in the 2nd revision, the interpretation relies on context. We appreciate the reviewer’s focus on the pifq context, but we do not agree that conclusions should be weighted primarily by this background. Our aim is to explain molecular mechanisms and physiological responses in wild-type plants, where partner factors are present. In the wild-type setting where partners are abundant, PIF4 variants with impaired TAD or DBD retain function, whereas eliminating oligomerization competence (mBH) abrogates output. The pifq data are useful precisely because they partially remove redundancy and reveal that PIF4’s intrinsic modules (TAD and presumably DBD) become more consequential; they do not, however, demonstrate that wild-type function relies heavily on homodimers or exclude partner-dependent assemblies.
As the reviewer pointed out, the mBH variant abolished more than oligomerization—it also disrupted DNA binding. We noted that in our original submission and thus included mB, which only disrupted DNA binding, as a control. Our comparison of mBH (no rescue) with mB (rescue in pif4) supports the importance of oligomerization competence without asserting that dimers are nonfunctional.
Operationally, we envision PIF4 recruiting partners as a pre-assembled homodimer or even homotetramer rather than as a monomer. Accordingly, our focus on hetero-oligomerization highlights partner-enabled activity; it does not preclude functional contributions from PIF4 homodimers/homooligomers.
To avoid further confusion, we have changed the last sentence of the Results (lines 455–458) to “Collectively, these data support a partner-dependent mechanism in which oligomerization competence is critical for robust thermomorphogenetic output, while PIF4’s transactivation and DNA-binding contributions can be supplied in trans when partners are available.”
References
1. Han, X. et al. Arabidopsis Transcription Factor TCP5 Controls Plant Thermomorphogenesis by Positively Regulating PIF4 Activity. iScience 15, 611–622 (2019).
We thank both reviewers for their constructive suggestions and great support, which helped us improve our manuscript.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_2: The authors have satisfactorily addressed all of my concerns. The revised manuscript now clearly presents the findings and avoids potential misinterpretation through the use of the term ‘supplied in trans.’

peer_review_rounds.author_response: Response: Thank you again for your wonderful suggestions that helped us revise the manuscript.

review_generation.input:
You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Plants tailor their architecture to warm temperatures through the central transcription factor
PHYTOCHROME-INTERACTING FACTOR 4 (PIF4). Here, we dissect how structured and
disordered regions of PIF4 contribute to its function in thermomorphogenesis. A long N-terminal
intrinsically disordered region (IDR) enables PIF4 to form low-mobility condensates. Within this IDR,
we identify an acidic transactivation domain (TAD) and an extended basic segment that carries a
nuclear-localization signal and the canonical basic motif of the basic helix-loop-helix (bHLH) domain.
The basic segment is both necessary and sufficient to drive PIF4 condensate formation, while the TAD
tunes condensate properties. Strikingly, alanine substitutions that abolish TAD-mediated transactivation,
disrupt DNA binding, or greatly reduce phase-separation propensity have no significant effect on
thermomorphogenetic hypocotyl elongation. By contrast, substituting twelve basic residues within the
basic segment, which disrupts both DNA binding and HLH-mediated oligomerization, abolishes
thermo-induced hypocotyl growth. These findings suggest that PIF4’s oligomerization competence
contributes significantly to thermomorphogenesis by enabling partner recruitment, allowing DNA-
binding and transactivation functions to be supplied in trans.

---

## Introduction

Plants react distinctly to different temperature regimes. Growth and development are severely impeded
at extreme heat or cold, as cell damage hinders normal physiological processes and energy and
resources are redirected from growth to stress tolerance and defense1,2. By contrast, within the non-
stressful ambient range (≈12–27 °C), moderate warming strongly remodels seedling morphology—
hypocotyls, roots, and petioles elongate, reshaping overall architecture in a process known as
thermomorphogenesis3,4. These changes are driven by multiple thermosensory transcription factors
(TTFs), which accumulate and/or activate as temperature rises and regulate genes involved in
phytohormone signaling and cell-wall modifications5,6.

Arabidopsis thaliana TTFs identified to date span multiple gene families, including but not limited to
PHYTOCHROME-INTERACTING FACTORs (PIFs), B-BOX proteins (BBXs), Class A1 HEAT
SHOCK FACTORs (HSFA1s), TEOSINTE BRANCHED 1/CYCLOSIDEA/PCF proteins (TCPs), and
BRASSINAZOLE RESISTANT 1 (BZR1)7–17. At the hub of their regulatory network is the basic Helix-
Loop-Helix (bHLH) transcription factor PIF4, as nearly every other TTF converges on its pathway by
modulating at least one aspect of PIF4—its transcription, DNA-binding, transcriptional activity, and
protein stability18. For example, BZR1 and TCP5 bind the PIF4 promoter and boost its expression upon
temperature elevation12,13,17, whereas thermo-induced nuclear accumulation of HSFA1s not only
enhances PIF4 transcription but also stabilizes PIF4 protein15,16. PIF4’s pivotal status in thermosensory
growth is underscored by its position immediately downstream of the two established thermosensors—
phytochrome B (phyB) and the evening-complex component ELF319–24. Multiple BBX proteins,
including BBX18, BBX23, BBX24, and BBX25, have been reported to promote PIF4-driven
thermomorphogenesis by physically interacting with and antagonizing ELF39–11.

PIF4’s centrality is unsurprising given that the eight-member PIF family (PIF1–PIF8) underpins
numerous pathways, including photomorphogenesis, shade avoidance, temperature signaling, and
immunity25–27. Acting as a signaling hub, PIF4 integrates diverse cues—light, temperature, drought,
salinity, and pathogen attack—and thereby mediates growth-defense trade-offs, a role exemplified by its
control of leaf senescence28–36. Yet, aside from two sequence features shared by all PIFs—an N-terminal
active phyB-binding (APB) motif that confers phyB interaction and a C-terminal bHLH domain for
DNA binding and oligomerization37, the sequence-function landscape of PIF4 remains largely
unexplored.

Eukaryotic transcription factors (TFs) are characterized by two core functions: a DNA-binding capacity
that recognizes specific sequences (e.g., cis-elements in promoters and enhancers) and a transactivation
activity that recruits cofactors to modulate transcription38,39. Accordingly, TFs are generally organized
into a DNA-binding domain (DBD) and one or more effector domains (EDs), such as transcriptional
activation domains (TADs) and repression domains (RDs)40–43. Many TFs also include auxiliary regions
that mediate protein-protein interactions (e.g., oligomerization) and other regulatory processes (e.g.,
post-translational modifications). These contacts with DNA or protein cofactors arise from both ordered
domains, such as DBDs or oligomerization domains, and intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) that
can adopt multiple conformations44. Mounting evidence shows that multivalent interactions among
IDRs drive phase separation to form biomolecular condensates that facilitate transcription45. Notably,
many TADs partition with the Mediator coactivator complex into such condensates, linking a TF’s
activation potential to the phase-separation propensity of its TAD46. Though some DBDs (e.g., zinc
finger and homeodomain) allow TFs to bind DNA as monomers, many TFs engage DNA as dimers or
higher-order oligomers47. This requirement is especially pronounced in the bHLH, bZIP, and MADS-
box families, whose noncovalent dimerization or oligomerization is a prerequisite for DNA binding.
Emerging evidence suggests that dimerization/oligomerization also contributes to the nuclear
condensate formation of several TFs48,49.

PIF4 is a typical bHLH TF. It carries a bipartite DBD: a basic stretch rich in arginines that contacts
DNA and an HLH module that drives both homo- and hetero-oligomerization50–52. Upon warm-
temperature cues, PIF4 accumulates in the nucleus and binds promoters of growth-related genes—
particularly those governing auxin biosynthesis and signaling, such as YUC8, IAA19, and IAA297,53,54.
PIF4 also physically engages several Mediator subunits, including MED14 and MED25, to activate
thermo-induced gene expression55,56, implying the existence of a functional TAD. In PIF3, a close
homolog, the transactivation activity maps to a p53-like TAD featured by a ΦxxΦΦ motif (Φ,
hydrophobic residues)57. Mutating this motif dramatically disrupts PIF3’s transcriptional activation
activity both in yeast and in planta, whereas an equivalent mutation in PIF4 only modestly reduces its
activity, leaving its precise TAD undefined. Recent work shows that PIF4 can phase separate with
JASMONATE ZIM-domain protein 3 (JAZ3), which restricts PIF4’s DNA-binding and transcriptional
activation activities58. However, whether PIF4 phase separation is indeed crucial for its
thermomorphogenetic function and whether the condensate formation relies on an as-yet-unmapped
TAD, its oligomeric bHLH core, or both remains unknown.

In this study, we dissect whether and how PIF4’s structured bHLH core and its “dark-matter” IDR
contribute to plant thermomorphogenesis. We uncover a long N-terminal IDR that forms low-mobility
condensates in vitro and in planta, yet these assemblies are temperature-insensitive and exhibit limited
fluidity. Interestingly, eliminating phase separation—by either mutating the acidic-type TAD or
substituting basic residues in the DNA-binding motif—barely impairs PIF4’s ability to restore warm
temperature-induced hypocotyl elongation in the pif4 mutant. By contrast, substituting twelve basic
residues, nine in the basic motif and three in the first helix of PIF4’s HLH domain, abolishes higher-
order oligomerization and extinguishes thermomorphogenetic growth. We therefore propose a partner-
dependent model of PIF4-mediated thermomorphogenetic regulation, in which PIF4’s ability to
oligomerize—potentially aided by its long N-terminal IDR—enables recruitment of cofactors that can
supply DNA-binding and transactivation in trans.
